Oncology is the branch of medicine concerned with the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. Mathematical models can be used to study how cancer develops, grows, and spreads. By providing quantitative and predictive frameworks, mathematical models allow hypotheses about cancer to be tested and evaluated. A carcinogen is any substance that causes cancer. Carcinogenesis is the process by which normal cells are transformed into cancer cells. A key observation that motivated many mathematical models of carcinogenesis is cancer incidence. Cancer incidence often increases rapidly with age, while the occurrence of cancer in an individual appears highly stochastic. However, patterns emerge when cancer incidence is examined across populations. These observations contributed to the development of multistage theories of carcinogenesis, which describe cancer development as a sequence of stages or changes in cells. Beginning in the 1920s, experiments involving chemical carcinogens provided evidence for the idea that cancer develops through multiple stages. In particular, applying two different carcinogens in sequence often produced higher cancer rates than applying a single carcinogen over time, leading to the two-stage model of carcinogenesis. Charles and Luce-Clausen developed one of the first quantitative multistage theories in the 1940s, using a mathematical model to describe the development of skin tumors in mice. Their work demonstrated how mathematical models could be used to connect assumptions about cellular changes with observed cancer incidence. Armitage and Doll further developed multistage theory in the 1950s, introducing more general mathematical models that allowed different rates for different stages and treated the stages as sequential cellular changes rather than necessarily genetic mutations. Their work helped establish mathematical modelling as a framework for studying the development of cancer. 1.3 What is a Mathematical Model? A mathematical model is a numerical representation of a real-world problem. By replacing physical experimentation with mathematical simulations, it allows researchers to evaluate system dynamics and predict future outcomes. 1.4 Systems of ODEs as Mathematical Models A system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) is a set of equations that involves two or more dependent variables that depend on one independent variable. A solution to this system is a set of functions that satisfies each equation on some interval \(I\). A system of ODEs can serve as a mathematical model by describing real world systems where multiple interacting components evolve over a shared independent variable. For example, in ecology, the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model uses a system of two coupled ODEs to track the interdependent population sizes of two interacting species over time \(t\). Many mathematical models are described using systems of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). It is useful to identify equilibrium points of a system of ODEs and study the stability of the equilibria. That is, an equilibrium point is a point at which both variables \(x\) and \(y\) remain constant over time. At an equilibrium, there is no net change in either variable. It is important to note that the equilibrium of a system does not mean that individual processes affecting \(x\) and \(y\) have stopped. Rather, the processes are balancing each other. Finding an equilibrium tells us where a system can remain unchanged, but does not tell us what happens if the system is slightly disturbed. Stability describes how a system behaves following a small deviation from an equilibrium. An equilibrium is stable if solutions that start sufficiently close to the equilibrium remain close to it. An equilibrium is asymptotically stable, if it is stable and solutions that start sufficiently close will eventually approach the equilibrium. An equilibrium is unstable if it is not stable. To study the local stability of an equilibrium \((x^*, y^*)\), we analyse the eigenvalues of \(J(x^*, y^*)\). If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both real and negative, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is asymptotically stable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both real and positive, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is unstable. If \(\lambda _ 1 < 0\) and \(\lambda_2 > 0\), with both being real, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is called a saddle point and is unstable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both complex with negative real parts, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is asymptotically stable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both complex with positive real parts, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is unstable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both purely imaginary, then the linearized system exhibits oscillatory behaviour. Further analysis is required to determine stability. Firstly, the activation term \(\alpha\) is simplistic and does not capture the complexities of immune responses to tumour growth. We also assumed proportional growth and decay, which is not realistic. Secondly, consider the case where there are no tumour cells (\(T=0\)). By (1.2), \( rac{dE}{dt}=-\delta E\). We get that \(E(t)= E(0)e^{-\delta t}\), implying that density of effector cells tends to zero over time. This is unrealistic, as effector cells are constantly present throughout the body. 2 The Kuznetsov Tumour–Immune Model 2.1 The Simple Kuznetsov Model A tumour is an abnormal mass of tissue that forms when cells grow and divide more than they should or do not die when they should. Tumours may be benign (not cancer) or malignant (cancer). Malignant tumours can spread into, or invade, nearby tissues. They can also spread to other parts of the body through the blood and lymph systems. Tumour cells reproduce and therefore could increase the tumour population. Moreover, tumour cells can also be removed through interactions with immune effector cells. These cells recognize and respond to abnormal cells, including tumour cells. Some examples of these cells are cytotoxic T lymphocytes and natural killer cells. Define the following: \(E\): Number of effector cells located at the tumor site, \(T\): Number of tumor cells located at the tumor site, \(s\): Baseline rate at which mature effector cells enter the tumour region, \(p\): Rate of tumour stimulated effector cell accumulation \(g\): Saturation parameter for tumour stimulated effector cell accumulation, \(m\): Rate of effector cell inactivation due to interactions with tumour cells, \(n\): Rate of tumour cell killing through interactions with effector cells, \(d\): Rate of ordinary effector cell elimination \(a\): Maximum growth rate of the tumor cell population, \(b\): Inverse of maximum carrying capacity, where all of the above parameters are constant. To determine the rate of change of the effector cell population, we consider processes that increase and decrease the number of effector cells. Effector cells enter the tumour region at baseline rate \(s\). Tumour cells also stimulate the accumulation of effector cells. We assume that this stimulation increases with tumour cell number but eventually saturates, giving the term \( rac{pET}{g+T}\). The saturation reflects the assumption that the accumulation of effector cells cannot increase indefinitely as tumour size increases, due to biological limitations. Effector cells are also inactivated through interactions with tumour cells at a rate proportional to both \(E\) and \(T\), giving the term \(mET\). Finally, effector cells are eliminated naturally at a rate proportional to the size of the population, giving the term \(dE\). Combining these processes together, we obtain: \[ egin{equation}  rac{dE}{dt} = s +  rac{pET}{g+T} - mET -dE 	ag{2.1} \end{equation}\] Similarly, to determine the rate of change of the tumour cell population, we consider processes that increase and decrease the number of tumour cells. We assume that tumour cells undergo logistic growth. At low tumour cell numbers, growth is approximately exponential, while at high tumour cell numbers, growth slows due to limitations such as available resources. This gives the logistic growth term \(aT(1-bT)\). Tumour cells are also removed through interactions with immune effector cells. We assume that the rate of tumour cell killing is proportional to both the number of tumour cells and the number of effector cells, giving the term \(nET\). Combining tumour growth and immune mediated killing, we obtain: \[ egin{equation}  rac{dT}{dt} = aT(1-bT) -nET 	ag{2.2} \end{equation}\] Equations (2.1) and (2.2) form the reduced Kuznetsov tumour immune model. These equations form a system of ODEs describing the interactions between tumour cells and immune effector cells. 2.2 Analysing the Kuznetsov Model Recall that an equilibrium is a state where both \( rac{dE}{dt}=0\) and \( rac{dT}{dt}=0\). However, the qualitative behaviour of the system may change when one or more model parameters are varied. Parameters such as tumour growth rates, immune response strength, and immune evasion may differ between individuals or change over time. Hence, it is important to consider how the model may change when we vary the parameters. A bifurcation occurs when a small change in a parameter causes a qualitative change in the behaviour of a dynamical system. These changes may include the appearance or disappearance of equilibrium points, or a change in the stability of an equilibrium. For the Kuznetsov model, parameters such as the maximum tumour growth rate \(a\), the tumour killing rate \(n\), and the rate of tumour-stimulated effector accumulation \(p\) may be treated as bifurcation parameters. Varying these parameters allows us to study how changes in tumour growth or immune activity affect the equilibria of the system. In particular, the parameter \(	heta\) represents the effectiveness of immune-mediated tumour killing relative to the original tumour population. A decrease in \(	heta\) therefore corresponds to increased immune resistance. By varying \(	heta\), we can examine whether increasing tumour resistance changes the number or stability of the equilibria. Bifurcation diagrams provide information that cannot be obtained from a single phase plane plot. A phase plane describes the behaviour of the system for one fixed set of parameters, whereas a bifurcation diagram describes how the long-term behaviour of the system changes across a range of parameter values. 2.6 Summary Starting from the two-population Kuznetsov tumor–immune model, we showed that its coexistence-equilibrium structure is governed by a cubic polynomial whose coefficient signs – not its explicit roots – determine whether the system is monostable or bistable. The same sign-test machinery, applied unchanged after remapping three parameters to account for a resistant phenotype, shows that an immune-resistant tumor subpopulation inherits the same qualitative bistability whenever effector activation continues to dominate tumor-induced exhaustion at the resistant phenotype’s parameter values. This worked example illustrates a general strategy for analyzing tumor–immune models in this course: reduce the equilibrium condition to a low-degree polynomial, and use a sign test on its coefficients, rather than brute-force root-finding, to characterize the number and type of biologically admissible steady states. % %

Tumours may be benign (not cancer) or malignant (cancer). Malignant tumours can spread into, or invade, nearby tissues. Figure 3.3: Phase portrait of the extended Kuznetsov model under reduced antigen presentation with theta = 0.7. 3.5 Bifurcation Analysis So far, we have studied the equilibria and stability of the Kuznetsov tumour-immune model for fixed parameter values. However, the qualitative behaviour of the system may change when one or more model parameters are varied. Parameters such as tumour growth rates, immune response strength, and immune evasion may differ between individuals or change over time. Hence, it is important to consider how the model may change when we vary the parameters. A bifurcation occurs when a small change in a parameter causes a qualitative change in the behaviour of a dynamical system. These changes may include the appearance or disappearance of equilibrium points, or a change in the stability of an equilibrium. For the Kuznetsov model, parameters such as the maximum tumour growth rate \(a\), the tumour killing rate \(n\), and the rate of tumour-stimulated effector accumulation \(p\) may be treated as bifurcation parameters. Varying these parameters allows us to study how changes in tumour growth or immune activity affect the equilibria of the system. In particular, the parameter \(	heta\) represents the effectiveness of immune-mediated tumour killing relative to the original tumour population. A decrease in \(	heta\) therefore corresponds to increased immune resistance. By varying \(	heta\), we can examine whether increasing tumour resistance changes the number or stability of the equilibria. Bifurcation diagrams provide information that cannot be obtained from a single phase plane plot. A phase diagram describes the behaviour of the system for one fixed set of parameters, whereas a bifurcation diagram describes how the long term behaviour of the system changes across a range of parameter values. The bifurcation diagrams illustrate how changes in model parameters affect the number and stability of equilibrium points. Figure 3.4 shows the effect of varying the baseline effector cell influx rate \(s\) in the original Kuznetsov model. For smaller values of \(s\), multiple positive equilibria exist, including two stable equilibria separated by an unstable saddle point. As \(s\) increases, some equilibria disappear through a saddle-node bifurcation. This demonstrates how increasing immune effector cells can change the long term behaviour of the tumour–immune system. Figures 3.5 and 3.6 illustrate the effects of immune resistance under reduced antigen presentation and immune checkpoint evasion, respectively. In both cases, \(	heta\) represents the effectiveness of immune-mediated tumour killing, with smaller values corresponding to greater resistance. Under reduced antigen presentation, increasing \(	heta\) can lead to the appearance of additional positive equilibria, while the checkpoint evasion model maintains multiple positive equilibria across the parameter range considered. These results demonstrate that different resistance mechanisms can affect the equilibrium structure differently, even when both reduce the effectiveness of immune-mediated tumour killing. 3.6 Summary Starting from the two-population Kuznetsov tumor–immune model, we showed that its coexistence-equilibrium structure is governed by a cubic polynomial whose coefficient signs – not its explicit roots – determine whether the system is monostable or bistable. The same sign-test machinery, applied unchanged after remapping three parameters to account for a resistant phenotype, shows that an immune-resistant tumor subpopulation inherits the same qualitative bistability whenever effector activation continues to dominate tumor-induced exhaustion at the resistant phenotype’s parameter values. This worked example illustrates a general strategy for analyzing tumor–immune models in this course: reduce the equilibrium condition to a low-degree polynomial, and use a sign test on its coefficients, rather than brute-force root-finding, to characterize the number and type of biologically admissible steady states. % %

5 Statistical Methods in Oncology 5.1 Review of Probability Distributions Probability distributions are fundamental to statistical modelling, as they describe the likelihood of different outcomes of random processes. In oncology, probability distributions are used to model various outcomes, including whether a patient develops cancer, the number of patients who respond to a treatment, and the time until disease recurrence or death. Different statistical methods rely on different probability distributions depending on the nature of the outcome being studied. 5.1.1 Random Variables and Probability Distributions A random variable is a function that assigns a real number to each outcome of a random experiment. Random variables may be classified as either discrete or continuous. A discrete random variable takes values on a finite or countable infinite set. Its distribution can be described by a probability mass function (PMF), \[ p_X(x)=P(X=x), \] which satisfies \(p_X(x)\geq 0\) and \(\sum_x p_X(x)=1.\) A continuous random variable takes values from an uncountable infinite set. A continuous random variable has a distribution that can be described by a probability density function (PDF), denoted by \(f_X(x)\), satisfying \(f_X(x)\geq 0\) and \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x)\,dx=1.\) For a continuous random variable, probabilities over intervals are calculated by integration. In particular, \[ P(a\leq X\leq b)=\int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx. \] Both discrete and continuous random variables can be described by their cumulative distribution function (CDF), \[ F_X(x)=P(X\leq x). \] The expected value and variance are used to describe the centre and variability of a probability distribution. The expected value of \(X\) is denoted by \(E(X)\), while its variance is defined as \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-E(X)^2]\), the expected squared deviation from the mean. Let \(X_1, X_2,...,X_n\) be indepedent random variables. Then, \[E(\sum_{i=1}^n c_i X_i)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i E(X_i), \] and \[\operatorname{Var} (\sum_{i=1}^n c_i X_i)= \sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2 \operatorname{Var} (X_i) \] We now introduce common discrete and continuous probability distributions and discuss their applications in oncology. 5.1.2 Discrete Probability Distributions 5.1.2.1 Bernoulli Distribution The Bernoulli distribution describes a random experiment with two possible outcomes, typically represented by \(0\) and \(1\). It is particularly useful for modelling binary outcomes. Let \(X\) be a Bernoulli random variable with parameter \(p\), where \(0\leq p\leq 1\). We write \(X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p).\) The probability mass function is \[ P(X=x)=p^x(1-p)^{1-x}, \qquad x=0,1. \] The expected value and variance are \(E(X)=p\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p)\). Suppose researchers are interested in whether a patient responds to a particular cancer treatment. Let \(X=1\) indicate that a patient responds to treatment and \(X=0\) indicate that the patient does not respond. If the probability of responding is \(p\), then \(X\) follows a Bernoulli distribution. The Bernoulli distribution is particularly important in logistic regression, where the probability of a binary outcome is modelled as a function of explanatory variables. 5.1.2.2 Binomial Distribution The binomial distribution describes the number of successes in a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials, each with the same probability of success. Let \(X\) denote the number of successes in \(n\) independent trials, each with probability of success \(p\). Then, \(X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)\). The probability mass function is \[ P(X=x)=\binom{n}{x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x}, \qquad x=0,1,\ldots,n. \] The expected value and variance are \(E(X)=np\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)\). Suppose a clinical trial involves \(100\) patients receiving a particular cancer treatment. If each patient independently responds with probability \(p=0.7\), then the number of patients who respond can be modelled as \(X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(100,0.7)\). The expected number of patients who respond is \(E(X)=100(0.7)=70\). Also, the probability that at least \(80\) patients respond to the treatment is \[ P(X \geq 80) = \sum_{x = 80}^{100} \binom{100}{x} (0.7)^x (0.3)^{100-x} \approx 0.01646285 \] 5.1.3 Continuous Probability Distributions 5.1.3.1 Normal Distribution The normal distribution is a continuous probability distribution characterized by its symmetric, bell-shaped density function. Let \(X\) follow a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), where \(\sigma>0\). We write \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2).\) Its probability density function is \[ f_X(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}} \exp\left( -\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right), \qquad -\infty<x<\infty. \] The expected value and variance are \(E(X)=\mu\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.\) If \(Z \sim N(0,1)\), we say \(Z\) follows a standard normal distribution. Also, if \(X_1,X_2,...,X_n\) are normal random variables, then \(\sum_{i=1}^n {c_i X_i}\) is also a normal random variable, where \(c_1,c_2,...,c_n \in \mathbb{R}\). That is, a linear combination of normal random variables is also normal. Figure 5.1: Normal distributions with different means and variances. 5.1.3.2 Chi-Squared Distribution The chi-squared distribution is a continuous probability distribution commonly used in statistical inference, particularly for hypothesis testing and estimating population variances. Let \(Z_1,Z_2,\ldots,Z_{n}\) be independent standard normal random variables, where \(n\) is a positive integer. Then the random variable \[ X=\sum_{i=1}^{n}Z_i^2 \] follows a chi-squared distribution with \(n\) degrees of freedom. We write \(X\sim\chi^2_{n}.\) Its probability density function is \[ f_X(x)= \frac{1}{2^{n/2}\Gamma(n/2)} x^{n/2-1}e^{-x/2}, \qquad x>0, \] where \(\Gamma(\cdot)\) denotes the gamma function. The expected value and variance are \(E(X)=n\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=2n.\) A very useful result is that \[ \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-1},\] where \(s^2\) is the sample variance, and \(\sigma^2\) is the population variance. The chi-squared distribution is nonnegative and generally right-skewed. Its shape depends on the degrees of freedom, becoming less skewed as the degrees of freedom increase. Figure 5.2: Chi-squared distributions with different degrees of freedom. 5.1.3.3 Student’s t-Distribution The Student’s t-distribution is a continuous probability distribution that is symmetric about zero and resembles the standard normal distribution. However, the t-distribution has heavier tails, allowing for greater variability and more extreme observations. It is particularly useful for statistical inference when the population variance is unknown. Let \(Z \sim N(0,1)\) and \(W \sim \chi^2_{n}\). Then \(X = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{\frac{W}{n}}}\) follows a Student’s t-distribution with \(n>0\) degrees of freedom. We write \(X\sim t_{n}.\) Its probability density function is \[ f_X(x)= \frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)} {\sqrt{n \pi}\Gamma\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)} \left(1+\frac{x^2}{n}\right)^{-\frac{n+1}{2}}, \qquad -\infty<x<\infty, \] where \(\Gamma(\cdot)\) denotes the gamma function and \(n\) represents the degrees of freedom. The expected value is \(E(X)=0,\qquad n>1,\) and the variance is \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{n}{n-2},\qquad n>2.\) The shape of the Student’s t-distribution depends on its degrees of freedom, denoted by \(n\). For smaller values of \(n\), the distribution has heavier tails and a lower peak compared to the standard normal distribution. As \(n\) increases, the tails become lighter and the distribution approaches the standard normal distribution. In particular, as \(n\to\infty\), the Student’s t-distribution converges in distribution to \(N(0,1)\). Figure 5.3: Student’s t-distributions with different degrees of freedom, compared with the standard normal distribution. Suppose researchers are interested in determining whether the mean tumour size differs between two independent groups of patients receiving different cancer treatments. Under suitable assumptions, a two-sample t-test may be used to investigate whether there is a statistically significant difference in mean tumour size between the groups. The t-distribution is also important in linear regression, where t-tests are commonly used to determine whether individual regression coefficients differ significantly from zero. For example, researchers may use a t-test to investigate whether a patient’s age is significantly associated with tumour size after accounting for other explanatory variables. We discuss this in further detail later in the chapter. 5.1.3.4 Exponential Distribution The exponential distribution is a continuous probability distribution frequently used to model waiting times until an event of interest occurs. Let \(X\) follow an exponential distribution with rate parameter \(\lambda>0\). We write \(X\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(\lambda).\) Its probability density function is \[ f_X(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}, \qquad x\geq 0. \] The expected value and variance are \(E(X)=\frac{1}{\lambda}\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{1}{\lambda^2}.\) The shape of the exponential distribution depends on its rate parameter, denoted by \(\lambda\). As \(\lambda\) increases, the probability density decreases more rapidly, indicating that shorter waiting times become more likely. Conversely, smaller values of \(\lambda\) correspond to longer expected waiting times. Since \(E(X)=1/\lambda\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/\lambda^2\), both the expected value and variance decrease as the rate parameter increases. Figure 5.4: Exponential distributions with different rate parameters. Moreover, the exponential distribution is important in survival analysis because it assumes a constant hazard function, \(h(t)=\lambda.\) Suppose researchers are interested in the time between cancer diagnosis and disease recurrence. Under the assumption that the instantaneous recurrence rate remains constant over time, the time until recurrence may be modelled using an exponential distribution. 5.1.3.5 Weibull Distribution The Weibull distribution is a continuous probability distribution commonly used to model time-to-event data. Unlike the exponential distribution, the Weibull distribution can accommodate hazard functions that increase or decrease over time. Let \(X\) follow a Weibull distribution with shape parameter \(k>0\) and scale parameter \(\lambda>0\). We write \(X\sim\operatorname{Weibull}(k,\lambda).\) Its probability density function is \[ f_X(x)= \frac{k}{\lambda} \left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1} \exp\left[-\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^k\right], \qquad x\geq 0. \] The expected value and variance are \(E(X)=\lambda\Gamma\left(1+\frac{1}{k}\right)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda^2\left[\Gamma\left(1+\frac{2}{k}\right)-\Gamma^2\left(1+\frac{1}{k}\right)\right]\) where \(\Gamma(\cdot)\) denotes the gamma function. Figure 5.5: Weibull distributions with different shape parameters and a fixed scale parameter. The Weibull distribution may be used to model the time from cancer diagnosis to death or disease recurrence when the risk of experiencing the event changes over time. For example, the Weibull distribution may be appropriate when the risk of recurrence decreases as time passes after treatment, provided that this pattern is supported by the observed data. 5.2 Simple Linear Regression Regression analysis is a statistical method used to study relationships between a response variable and one or more explanatory variables. In oncology, regression models can be used to study relationships between patient characteristics, treatment-related factors, and clinical outcomes. Simple linear regression (SLR) examines the relationship between a continuous response variable and an explanatory variable by assuming that their relationship is linear. Understanding SLR provides a foundation for more complex statistical models, including multiple linear regression and logistic regression. 5.2.1 The Simple Linear Regression Model Let \(Y_i\) denote the response variable for observation \(i\) and let \(x_i\) denote the corresponding explanatory variable. The simple linear regression model is defined as \[ Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i, \qquad i=1,\ldots,n, \] where: \(Y_i\) is the response variable for observation \(i\). \(x_i\) is the explanatory variable for observation \(i\). \(\beta_0\) is the population intercept. \(\beta_1\) is the population slope. \(\varepsilon_i\) is the random error associated with observation \(i\). \(n\) is the number of observations. The population regression coefficients \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are generally unknown and must be estimated using observed data. Their estimates are denoted by \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\), respectively. The fitted regression equation is \[ \hat{Y}_i=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1x_i, \] where \(\hat{Y}_i\) represents the predicted value of the response variable for observation \(i\). Note that a linear association between the response and explanatory variables does not imply a causal relationship between them. A residual is the difference between an observed response and its predicted value. For observation \(i\), the residual is defined as \[ e_i=Y_i-\hat{Y}_i. \] Substituting the fitted regression equation gives \[ e_i=Y_i-\hat{\beta}_0-\hat{\beta}_1x_i. \] The residual sum of squares is defined by \[ Q= \sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2. \] The objective of ordinary least squares is to find values of \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) that minimize \(Q\). We begin with \[ Q= \sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2. \] Taking the partial derivative with respect to \(\beta_0\) gives \[ \frac{\partial Q}{\partial\beta_0} = -2\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i). \] Setting this derivative equal to zero and evaluating at the least squares estimates, \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i-\hat{\beta}_0-\hat{\beta}_1x_i)=0. \] Expanding, \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n}Y_i -n\hat{\beta}_0 -\hat{\beta}_1\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=0. \] Rearranging and dividing by \(n\), we get, \[ \boxed{ \hat{\beta}_0=\bar{Y}-\hat{\beta}_1\bar{x} } \] where \(\bar{Y}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}Y_i\) and \(\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i.\) Now, taking the partial derivative with respect to \(\beta_1\) gives \[ \frac{\partial Q}{\partial\beta_1} = -2\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i(Y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i). \] Setting this derivative equal to zero, \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i(Y_i-\hat{\beta}_0-\hat{\beta}_1x_i)=0. \] Substituting the expression for \(\hat{\beta}_0\), \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \left[ Y_i-\bar{Y} +\hat{\beta}_1\bar{x} -\hat{\beta}_1x_i \right]=0. \] Rearranging, \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i(Y_i-\bar{Y}) = \hat{\beta}_1 \sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i(x_i-\bar{x}). \] we obtain \[ \boxed{ \hat{\beta}_1= \frac{ \sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})(Y_i-\bar{Y}) }{ \sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2 } }, \] Since \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i(Y_i-\bar{Y}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})(Y_i-\bar{Y})\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i(x_i-\bar{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2.\) Therefore, the least squares estimators are \[ \boxed{ \hat{\beta}_1= \frac{ \sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})(Y_i-\bar{Y}) }{ \sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2 } = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}} } \] and \[ \boxed{ \hat{\beta}_0=\bar{Y}-\hat{\beta}_1\bar{x}. }, \] where \(S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2\) and \(S_{xy}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})(Y_i-\bar{Y})\). Substituting these estimates into the regression equation gives the fitted model \[ \hat{Y}_i=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1x_i. \] We wish to fit the prostate cancer data. Using Table 5.1, we obtain \(\bar{x}= 1.35001,\) \(\bar{y}= 2.478387,\) \(S_{xx}= 133.359,\) and \(S_{xy}= 95.92784\). Plugging these values into the OLS estimators for \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), we get \[ \boxed{\hat{\beta_1} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}=\frac{95.92784}{133.359} \approx 0.7193} \] \[ \boxed{\hat{\beta_0}= \bar{Y}- \hat{\beta_1}\bar{x}= 2.478387 - (0.7193)(1.35001) \approx 1.5073} \] Hence, the estimated regression line is \(\hat{Y_i} = 1.5073 + 0.7193x_i\) 5.2.3 Interpretation of Regression Coefficients After estimating the regression coefficients, it is important to interpret their values in the context of the research question. The intercept \(\beta_0\) represents the expected value of the response variable when the explanatory variable is zero. The slope \(\beta_1\) represents the change in the expected response variable associated with a one-unit increase in the explanatory variable. A positive slope indicates that the expected response increases as the explanatory variable increases, while a negative slope indicates that the expected response decreases. Using the prostate cancer dataset, we obtain the following fitted regression model: \[ \widehat{\log(\text{PSA})} = 1.5073+0.7193\log(\text{Tumour Volume}), \] where PSA denotes prostate-specific antigen levels and tumour volume is measured in \(\text{cm}^3\). The estimated intercept is \(\hat{\beta}_0=1.5073\), indicating that when tumour volume is \(1\text{ cm}^3\), the predicted log PSA level is \(1.5073\). Exponentiating, we obtain \(e^{1.5073}\approx 4.51\). Thus, when tumour volume is \(1\text{ cm}^3\), the model predicts a PSA level of approximately \(4.51\) on the original scale. The estimated slope is \(\hat{\beta}_1=0.7193\). Since both variables are logarithmically transformed, a \(1\%\) increase in tumour volume is associated with an approximately \(0.7193\%\) increase in the predicted PSA level, according to the fitted model. For example, a patient with a tumour volume of \(5\text{ cm}^3\) would have a predicted log PSA level of \[ \widehat{\log(\text{PSA})} =1.5073+0.7193\log(5) \approx 2.665. \] Exponentiating gives \[ \widehat{\text{PSA}}=e^{2.665}\approx 14.37. \] Thus, the model predicts a median PSA level of approximately \(14.37\) on the original scale for a patient with a tumour volume of \(5\text{ cm}^3\). 5.2.4 Assumptions of Simple Linear Regression To interpret the regression model appropriately and perform statistical inference, several assumptions regarding the relationship between the variables and the behaviour of the error terms must be considered. Since the true errors are unobservable, residuals are commonly used to assess whether these assumptions are reasonable. 1. Linearity The expected response is assumed to be a linear function of the explanatory variable. If the true relationship is nonlinear, the linear model may provide an inadequate description of the data. Linearity can be assessed using a scatterplot of the response against the explanatory variable, or a plot of residuals against fitted values. If the linearity assumption is reasonable, the residuals should be randomly scattered around zero without a systematic pattern. A pattern may indicate that a nonlinear model is more appropriate. For the prostate cancer dataset, the scatterplot in Figure 5.6 suggests a positive relationship between log tumour volume and log PSA levels. The residual plot in Figure 5.7 appears to be randomly scattered, demonstrating no strong systematic departure from linearity. Thus, the linearity assumption appears reasonable. 2. Independence The error terms are assumed to be independent across observations. This assumption may be violated when repeated measurements are collected from the same patient, or when observations are correlated due to shared characteristics or clinical settings. Independence is primarily assessed by examining how the data were collected. For the prostate cancer dataset, each observation corresponds to a different patient. Therefore, independence appears reasonable, assuming that the patients were sampled independently and that no other sources of dependence are present. 3. Constant Variance (Homoscedasticity) The variance of the errors is assumed to be constant across all values of the explanatory variable. If the variability of the errors changes with the explanatory variable, the model exhibits heteroscedasticity. This assumption can be assessed using a plot of residuals against fitted values. Under constant variance, the vertical spread of the residuals should remain approximately the same across the range of fitted values. For the prostate cancer dataset, the spread of residuals appears relatively consistent across fitted values in Figure 5.7, suggesting that the constant variance assumption is reasonable. 4. Normality of Errors The error terms are assumed to follow a normal distribution: \[ \varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2). \] Normality can be assessed using a normal Q-Q plot of the residuals. If the errors are approximately normally distributed, the points should lie reasonably close to the reference line. Substantial departures from this line may indicate violations of normality. For the prostate cancer dataset, the normal Q-Q plot in Figure 5.7 shows that most residuals lie reasonably close to the reference line, with some deviations in the tails. Thus, the normality assumption appears reasonable for this example, though not perfect. Note that the normality assumption is not required to calculate the least squares estimates. However, it is used to justify hypothesis tests and confidence intervals. Overall, the diagnostic results suggest that the assumptions of simple linear regression are reasonably plausible for the log-transformed prostate cancer dataset, although some minor deviations are present. Figure 5.7: Diagnostic plots for the regression model relating log tumour volume to log PSA levels. 5.2.5 Coefficient of Determination (\(R^2\)) After fitting a simple linear regression model, it is important to evaluate how well the fitted regression line describes the observed data. One commonly used measure of model fit is the coefficient of determination, denoted by \(R^2\). To define \(R^2\), we first decompose the total variability in the response variable into variability explained by the regression model and unexplained residual variability. The total sum of squares (SST) measures the total observed variability in the response variable about its sample mean: \[ SST=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-\bar{Y})^2. \] The regression sum of squares (SSR) measures the variability accounted for by the fitted regression model: \[ SSR=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{Y}_i-\bar{Y})^2. \] The error sum of squares (SSE), also referred to as the residual sum of squares, measures the variability not explained by the fitted regression model: \[ SSE=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-\hat{Y}_i)^2. \] The identity \(SST=SSR+SSE\) can be established algebraically using the properties of the least squares estimators. We omit the derivation here for conciseness. The coefficient of determination is defined as the proportion of total observed variability in the response variable accounted for by the fitted regression model: \[ \boxed {R^2=\frac{SSR}{SST} = 1-\frac{SSE}{SST}}. \] Notice that \(0\leq R^2\leq 1\) An \(R^2\) value closer to one indicates that the fitted regression model accounts for a greater proportion of the observed variability in the response variable. Conversely, an \(R^2\) value closer to zero indicates that the model accounts for relatively little of the observed variability. Using the prostate cancer data in Table 5.1, we can compute \(SSE = 58.91476\) and \(SST = 127.9176\). We get that \(R^2 = 1 - \frac{58.91476}{127.9176}= 0.5394319\). This indicates that approximately \(53.94\%\) of the total variation in log PSA levels is explained by the linear relationship with log tumour volume. The remaining \(46.06\%\) of the variation is not explained by the model and may be associated with other factors or random variability. 5.2.6 Statistical Inference in Simple Linear Regression Least squares estimation provides estimates of the unknown regression coefficients \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). However, these estimates are calculated from a sample and are therefore subject to sampling variability. Statistical inference allows us to quantify this uncertainty and draw conclusions about the population regression parameters. Recall the simple linear regression model \[ Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i, \qquad i=1,\ldots,n, \] where the explanatory variable values \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) are treated as fixed, and the error terms are assumed to be independent and identically distributed according to \(\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\). Consequently,\(Y_i\sim N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2).\) 5.2.6.1 Sampling Distribution of the Slope Estimator Recall that the least squares estimator of the slope is \[ \hat{\beta}_1= \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})(Y_i-\bar{Y})} {\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2}, \] We can express \(\hat{\beta}_1\) as a linear combination of the response variables \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\). Define \[ c_i=\frac{x_i-\bar{x}}{S_{xx}}. \] Then, \[ \begin{aligned} \hat{\beta}_1 &=\frac{1}{S_{xx}} \sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})(Y_i-\bar{Y})\\ &=\frac{1}{S_{xx}} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})Y_i -\bar{Y}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x}) \right]. \end{aligned} \] Since \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})=0,\) we obtain \[ \hat{\beta}_1 =\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{x_i-\bar{x}}{S_{xx}}Y_i = \sum_{i=1}^{n}c_iY_i. \] Since \(\hat{\beta}_1\) is a linear combination of independent normally distributed random variables, it also follows a normal distribution. The expectation of \(\hat{\beta}_1\) can be found as follows: \[ \begin{aligned} E[\hat{\beta}_1] &=E\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_iY_i\right]\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_iE[Y_i]\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\\ &=\beta_0\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i +\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_ix_i\\ &= \beta_1 \end{aligned} \] Since \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i &=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{x_i-\bar{x}}{S_{xx}}\\ &=\frac{1}{S_{xx}} \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i-n\bar{x}\right)\\ &=0, \end{aligned} \] and \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^{n}c_ix_i &=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{x_i(x_i-\bar{x})}{S_{xx}}\\ &=\frac{1}{S_{xx}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[(x_i-\bar{x})+\bar{x}\right] (x_i-\bar{x})\\ &=\frac{1}{S_{xx}} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2 +\bar{x}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x}) \right]\\ &=\frac{S_{xx}}{S_{xx}}\\ &=1. \end{aligned} \] Hence, \[ \boxed{E[\hat{\beta}_1]=\beta_1.} \] Next, we derive the variance of \(\hat{\beta}_1\). Since the observations are independent and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\sigma^2\), \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1) &=\operatorname{Var}\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n}c_iY_i \right)\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i^2\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)\\ &=\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i^2. \end{aligned} \] Also, \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i^2 &=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{(x_i-\bar{x})^2}{S_{xx}^2}\\ &=\frac{1}{S_{xx}^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2\\ &=\frac{S_{xx}}{S_{xx}^2}\\ &=\frac{1}{S_{xx}}. \end{aligned} \] Hence, \[ \boxed{ \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1) =\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}. } \] Since \(\hat{\beta}_1\) is normally distributed, with expected value \(\beta_1\) and variance \(\sigma^2/S_{xx}\), we conclude that \[ \boxed{ \hat{\beta}_1\sim N\left(\beta_1,\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\right). } \] 5.2.6.2 Hypothesis Testing and Confidence Intervals for the Slope A common objective in regression analysis is to determine whether the explanatory variable has a statistically significant linear association with the response variable. To do this, we may test the hypotheses \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) against \(H_1:\beta_1\neq 0.\) We wish to use the sampling distribution derived above, however \(\sigma^2\) is usually unknown. It can be shown that \(\hat{\sigma^2} = \frac{SSE}{n-2}\) is an unbiased estimator for \(\sigma^2\). We omit the proof for conciseness. Thus, we estimate \(\sigma^2\) with \(\hat{\sigma}^2\). Further, it can be shown that \(\frac{SSE}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-2}\). The proof is beyond the scope of the text. Consider \(T=\frac{\hat{\beta_1}-\beta_1}{\sqrt{\frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{S_{xx}}}}\). Dividing the numerator and denominator by \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt {S_{xx}}}\), we get \[ T= \frac {\frac{\hat{\beta_1}- \beta_1}{\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt {S_{xx}}}}} {\sqrt{\frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2}}} \] Since \(\hat{\beta_1} \sim N(\beta_1, \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} )\), \(\frac{\hat{\beta_1}- \beta_1}{\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt {S_{xx}}}} \sim N(0,1).\) Also, \(\sqrt{\frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{\sigma^2}} = \sqrt{\frac{SSE}{(n-2)\sigma^2}}\). Since \(\frac{SSE}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-2}\), it follows that \(T \sim t_{n-2}\). That is, \[T=\frac{\hat{\beta_1}-\beta_1}{\sqrt{\frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{S_{xx}}}} \sim t_{n-2}\] Under \(H_0\), we substitute \(\beta_1=0\) to obtain the test statistic \[ \boxed{T^*=\frac{\hat{\beta_1}}{\sqrt{\frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{S_{xx}}}} } \] Under the null hypothesis, \(T^*\sim t_{n-2}.\) Rejecting \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) provides statistical evidence of a linear association between the explanatory and response variables under the assumptions of the regression model. However, statistical significance does not necessarily imply practical significance or a causal relationship. For a confidence level of \(100(1-\alpha)\%\), we have \[ P\left( -t_{n-2,1-\alpha/2} \leq \frac{\hat{\beta}_1-\beta_1}{\sqrt{\frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{S_{xx}}}} \leq t_{n-2,1-\alpha/2} \right)=1-\alpha. \] Multiplying through by the positive standard error, \[ P\left( -t_{n-2,1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{S_{xx}}} \leq \hat{\beta}_1-\beta_1 \leq t_{n-2,1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{S_{xx}}} \right)=1-\alpha. \] Rearranging to isolate \(\beta_1\), \[ P\left( \hat{\beta}_1-t_{n-2,1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{S_{xx}}} \leq\beta_1\leq \hat{\beta}_1+t_{n-2,1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{S_{xx}}} \right)=1-\alpha. \] Therefore, a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) is \[ \boxed{ \hat{\beta}_1 \pm t_{n-2,1-\alpha/2} \frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}. } \] Suppose we wanted to test \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) against \(H_1:\beta_1\neq 0\) for the prostate cancer data, at the \(0.05\) significance level. Recall, \(\hat{\beta_1} = 0.7193\), \(S_{xx}= 133.359\), and \(SSE = 58.91476\). Also, \(n=97\), so \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{58.91476}{95} \approx 0.6202.\) Putting this together, \[T^* = \frac{0.7193}{\sqrt{\frac{0.6202}{133.359}}} \approx 10.5476. \] For a \(t\) distribution with \(95\) degrees of freedom, the rejection region is \(R^* = \{T : |T| > 1.985\}\) Since \(T^* \in R^*\), we reject the null in favour of the alternative. That is, we have statistically significant evidence that there is a linear association between log PSA levels and log tumour volume. A 95% confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) is \[ 0.7193 \pm 1.985 {\sqrt{\frac{0.6202}{133.359}}} = \boxed {(0.5839, 0.8547).} \] We are 95% confident that the true population slope lies between \(0.5839\) and \(0.8547\). Since both variables are logarithmically transformed, this suggests that a 1% increase in tumour volume is associated with an approximately 0.5839% to 0.8547% increase in PSA levels, on average. Furthermore, since the confidence interval does not contain zero, there is evidence of a statistically significant positive linear relationship between log tumour volume and log PSA levels at the 5% significance level, further verifying the result found in our hypothesis test.
